section.title: Paul's Ministry and Travel Plans
section.sectionRationale: Having reached the summit of his argument, Paul turns personal. He explains why he wrote so boldly to a church he did not found: because of the grace God gave him to be a minister of Christ to the Gentiles, a priestly service in which the nations become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Spirit. He describes his ambition to preach where Christ was not named, lays out his plan to visit Rome on the way to Spain after delivering the collection to the poor saints in Jerusalem, and asks earnestly for prayer, closing with the blessing of the God of peace.
section.thesis: Paul's whole apostolic labor is a priestly ministry of the gospel by which the Gentiles are offered up to God, sanctified by the Spirit; and this God-centered mission shapes his ambition, his travel plans, and his humble request for the prayers of the church, all resting in the God of peace.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Paul's bold reminder and his priestly ministry to the Gentiles; his ambition to preach where Christ was not named; his travel plans by way of Rome to Spain after the collection for Jerusalem; and his request for prayer and the blessing of the God of peace.

units.label: A priestly ministry to the Gentiles
units.note: the Gentiles an offering acceptable to God

verses.text: I myself am convinced, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, brimming with knowledge, and able to instruct one another.
However, I have written you a bold reminder on some points, because of the grace God has given me

to be a {{leitourgos|minister}} of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the {{hierourgeo|priestly service}} of the gospel of God, so that the Gentiles might become an {{prosphora|offering}} acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.
Therefore I exult in Christ Jesus in my service to God.

units.label: Ambition to preach where Christ is not named

verses.text: I will not presume to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me in leading the Gentiles to obedience by word and deed,
by the power of signs and wonders, and by the power of the Spirit of God. So from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ.
In this way I have aspired to preach the gospel where Christ was not known, so that I would not be building on someone else’s {{themelios|foundation}}.
Rather, as it is written: “Those who were not told about Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”
That is why I have often been hindered from coming to you.

units.label: Travel plans by way of Rome to Spain
units.note: the collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem

verses.text: But now that there are no further opportunities for me in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to visit you,
I hope to see you on my way to Spain. And after I have enjoyed your company for a while, you can equip me for my journey.
Now, however, I am on my way to Jerusalem to serve the saints there.
For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem.
They were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings, they are obligated to minister to them with material blessings.
So after I have completed this service and have safely delivered this bounty to them, I will set off to Spain by way of you.
I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.

units.label: A request for prayer and the God of peace
units.note: join me in my struggle by praying to God

verses.text: Now I urge you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to join me in my struggle by praying to God for me.
Pray that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service in Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints there,
so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and together with you be refreshed.
The God of {{eirene|peace}} be with all of you. Amen.

leitourgos.gloss: A minister or public servant, often with a sacred, priestly sense; the related words describe temple service and worship. Paul casts himself as a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving at the altar of the gospel. His apostolic labor is not merely administrative but priestly, offering up the nations to God.

hierourgeo.gloss: To perform sacred service, to work as a priest, to minister in holy things. Paul uses this striking priestly verb of his preaching of the gospel: proclaiming Christ is his altar work. The temple imagery reframes evangelism as worship, in which the herald serves God by bringing the nations near.

prosphora.gloss: An offering, that which is presented or brought to God, especially a sacrifice. The converted Gentiles are themselves the offering Paul brings to the altar, made acceptable to God and set apart by the Holy Spirit. The fruit of the gospel is a living sacrifice of redeemed people presented to God for His glory.

themelios.gloss: A foundation, the base on which a building rests. Paul aspired to preach where Christ was not yet named, so as not to build on another's foundation but to lay the gospel's groundwork in unreached places. The image fits his pioneering, frontier ambition to carry the good news to the ends of the earth.

eirene.gloss: Peace, wholeness, well-being; the Hebrew shalom stands behind it. Paul closes with the God of peace, the God who reconciles enemies to Himself and to one another through Christ. In a letter that heals division between strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, the blessing of the God of peace is the fitting seal.

basic.context: Paul now explains himself. Why write so boldly to a church he had never visited? Because God gave him grace to be the apostle to the Gentiles. He describes his ministry in priestly terms: preaching the gospel is his altar service, and the converted nations are the offering he brings to God. He tells of his ambition to reach unreached places, his plan to visit Rome on the way to Spain after taking a relief gift to Jerusalem, and his heartfelt request for prayer.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the personal, missionary close of the letter's body. Read it to see how doctrine drives mission and prayer. The priestly language of verse 16 is deliberate: evangelism is worship, and people are the sacrifice. The travel plans are not filler; they show the collection uniting Gentile and Jewish believers and reveal Paul's dependence on God and on the prayers of the church.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul calls himself a leitourgos, a priestly minister of Christ, engaged in hierourgeo, the sacred service of the gospel, so that the Gentiles become a prosphora, an offering acceptable to God. He aspired not to build on another's themelios, foundation, but to reach the unreached. And he ends with the God of eirene, peace, be with you all.
basic.typology: The temple, the altar, and the sacrifices find a new fulfillment: the gospel is the priestly service, and redeemed people are the offering. The relief gift for Jerusalem echoes the promise that the wealth of the nations would flow to Zion. Paul's mission to the ends of the earth carries forward Israel's calling to be a light to the nations.
basic.christ: Paul does not presume to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through him. Christ is the content of his preaching, the power behind his mission, and the one in whom he exults. He comes to Rome in the fullness of the blessing of Christ. The whole enterprise is Christ's work through His servant, leading the nations to the obedience of faith.
basic.god: The ministry is the priestly service of the gospel of God, and its aim is an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Spirit. Paul serves God, exults before God, plans by the will of God, and begs prayer to God. The passage is saturated with dependence on God, closing with the God of peace, whose reconciling character crowns the letter.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 52 stands behind Paul's ambition to reach those who had not heard. Romans 12 called believers to present themselves as a living sacrifice, which the priestly imagery here echoes. First Corinthians 16 and Second Corinthians 8 and 9 describe the same Jerusalem collection. Philippians 4 speaks of the God of peace.
basic.oneStory: God had promised that the nations would come to His light and that their gifts would flow to Zion. Here Paul, priest of the gospel, is gathering that harvest: the Gentiles offered up to God, a relief gift binding the nations to Jerusalem, and the good news pressing on to the ends of the earth. The one story of God moves outward through Paul toward Spain and beyond, carried by the God of peace.

context.literary:
Paul has been writing in the second person plural for fourteen chapters and in 15:14 he changes the key. 'I myself am convinced' opens a section in which the letter looks at its own writing. The section runs in four movements. Verses 14 to 21 explain why he has written, and look back over his ministry. Verses 22 to 29 look ahead and set out his travel plans in order: Jerusalem first, then Rome, then Spain. Verses 30 to 32 turn to prayer and ask for the Romans' help. Verse 33 closes with a benediction that stands as the end of the main body of the letter.

The passage is carefully balanced between modesty and boldness. It begins with a courtesy, 'you yourselves are full of goodness, brimming with knowledge', then admits to boldness, 'I have written you a bold reminder on some points'. It claims large results, 'from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum', then qualifies at once, 'I will not presume to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me'. Paul is making a case that he has the right to come to Rome without implying that Rome needs him to correct it. The social grammar of an ancient letter appears in miniature: reassure, explain, request.

The passage also makes an inclusio with the letter's opening. In 1:8 to 15 Paul had said he longed to see them and had been prevented from coming, and that he was eager to preach the gospel in Rome as well. In 15:22 he gives the reason for the delay, and in 15:23 and 24 he says the time has come. The thanksgiving and the travelogue frame the long theological argument between them. Readers who have just been through chapters of doctrine are now shown what the doctrine is for: it exists to send people out.
context.historical:
At this point in his career Paul is nearing the end of a long mission around the eastern Mediterranean. He writes in the winter or early spring of about AD 56 to 57, most likely from Corinth. Illyricum, the Roman province along the east side of the Adriatic, marks the western edge of what he has covered so far, and the route he describes runs in an arc from Jerusalem through Syria, Asia Minor, Macedonia and Achaia. Luke's account in Acts has no mention of Illyricum, so it is probably the edge of Macedonia or a stretch of preaching not recorded there.

His next plan is to go to Spain, which in the Roman world was the far west, a region of cities already Latin speaking and organised under Roman law. A mission there needed a base, and Rome was the natural one. He wants the Roman church to equip him for the journey, a phrase that in the early church referred to practical help with supplies, companions and introductions, as in 3 John 6 and Titus 3:13.

Before any of that, he must go to Jerusalem. The collection he is carrying came from churches in Macedonia and Achaia, and from Galatia and Asia, 1 Corinthians 16:1 to 4 and 2 Corinthians 8 and 9. It answered a request made at the Jerusalem meeting that Paul remember the poor, Galatians 2:10. Jerusalem in the 50s was tense. Some Jewish believers were suspicious of Paul, and the unbelieving authorities were hostile, which is why he asks for prayer to be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, 15:31. Luke in Acts 20 and 21 records how the visit unfolded: a plot against him as he sailed, then riots in the temple precinct and arrest.
context.canonical:
The priestly language of verse 16 is rooted in Isaiah 66:18 to 21. There the LORD promises to send survivors to the nations that have not heard of His fame, and they will bring all your brothers from all the nations as a gift to the LORD, 'just as the Israelites bring an offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD', and some of them will be taken as priests and Levites. Paul's picture of himself as the minister who presents the Gentiles as an acceptable offering reads like a conscious fulfilment of that oracle.

Verse 21 quotes Isaiah 52:15, from the passage that leads into the Suffering Servant's song. Kings who had not heard will see, and the nations who had not been told will understand. Paul uses it for a purpose that moves from prophecy to calling: he takes the hope of the prophet as his mission statement. The same pattern occurs in 2 Corinthians 10:15 and 16, where he speaks of preaching 'in the regions beyond you', and in 1 Corinthians 3:10 to 11, where he is the master builder who laid a foundation that is Christ.

The collection brings together several New Testament strands. It answers Galatians 2:10, and it is the subject of 1 Corinthians 16, 2 Corinthians 8 and 9, and the notice in Acts 24:17 that he came to Jerusalem to bring alms to his people. Second Corinthians 9:12 and 13 states its purpose, that it would produce thanksgiving to God and bring glory to Him through the saints' praise.

Finally, 15:33 begins a series of Pauline benedictions to 'the God of peace', repeated in 16:20, Philippians 4:9 and 1 Thessalonians 5:23, and echoed in Hebrews 13:20. The title is not decoration. In a letter that has been about the end of hostility between God and humanity and between Jew and Gentile, it names the God who brings it about.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's first aim is to remove an obstacle. A church he has never visited might fairly wonder why a stranger had written them such a weighty letter. He answers that he did so because of the grace God gave him and that his purpose is to serve them, not to take them over. His courtesy is real: he thinks well of them. But his mission is also real, and he intends that they should share it. The warm opening to the passage, 'you yourselves are full of goodness', is not a polite lie but a friendly assumption of maturity.

He also wants to enlist them. The final section of the passage is a request for money and prayer, and it has been prepared by the whole letter. If Gentile Christians in Rome have learned in chapters 1 to 11 that they owe their salvation to a Jewish Messiah, and in 14 and 15 that they must accept those unlike them, then it makes sense for them to join in a project that sends Gentile gifts to Jewish believers and sends the gospel to the far west.

Thirdly, he shows them how a servant of God sees his life. The ministry is not his own achievement. 'Christ has accomplished through me', the Spirit's power, signs and wonders, the unevangelised target, the delay for the sake of the work, the dangers ahead, all are set in the light of God's will, 15:32. The reader is meant to take away a way of looking at Christian service.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost all of the passage is description. It tells us what Paul has done and means to do, and no sentence in it commands a given pattern of missionary strategy. The risk is to treat his ambition to preach where Christ was not named, 15:20, as a rule for every church worker. Paul himself did not hold that rule for everyone. Priscilla and Aquila, Apollos and many others built on foundations he or others had laid, and he calls Apollos a fellow worker who watered what he planted, 1 Corinthians 3:6. What he describes is his own calling, and that calling is a pattern, but it is not a rulebook.

What does carry forward is the character of the ministry. It begins with grace, 15:15. It treats people as an offering and not a possession, 15:16. It speaks only of what Christ has done, 15:18. It works with dependence on prayer, 15:30 to 32, and it takes the needs of the poor seriously, 15:25 to 27. A church can learn from those marks without copying the geography.

The passage also needs care at 15:19, which speaks of signs and wonders. It tells us what accompanied his ministry. It does not promise the same signs in every case, and it ascribes them wholly to the power of the Spirit and not to Paul.

debates.question: What was the collection for?

views.label: Relief for the poor believers in Jerusalem
views.case: The plain reading of 15:25 to 27 and Galatians 2:10 is that it was to help the poor among the saints, and Paul calls it a ministry of service that supplies their needs, 2 Corinthians 9:12. The Gentiles had received spiritual blessings from Jerusalem and owed material help in return, Romans 15:27.

views.label: A sign of unity between Jew and Gentile
views.case: Some stress that Paul pressed the collection hard, took delegates from the Gentile churches to deliver it, and said it would prompt the saints to glorify God, 2 Corinthians 9:13. They see it as a demonstration that Gentile churches were part of the one family and not a separate religion.

views.label: The pilgrimage of the nations to Zion
views.case: A third view reads the gifts against Isaiah 60:5 to 6 and 66:20, where the wealth of the nations flows to Jerusalem. On this reading Paul sees himself bringing in the eschatological offering of the Gentiles. The priestly language of 15:16 and the 'bounty' of 15:28 fit this.

debates.bearing: The views are not rivals. Paul can do a very practical thing, relieve poverty, and attach to it the hope that the practical gift signifies something bigger. All three readings leave the same lesson: the church's material generosity belongs to its worship and its unity.

debates.question: Did Paul reach Spain?

views.label: Yes, after release from the Roman imprisonment of Acts 28
views.case: Early Christian tradition, including a first century letter from Rome to Corinth that speaks of him reaching the limit of the west, and a later document known as the Muratorian fragment, reports the journey. Those who accept it place it after the two years of Acts 28:30.

views.label: The evidence is too thin to say
views.case: Others note that Acts is silent and that Paul's later letters, the Pastorals, speak of travel in the east, Titus 1:5 and 2 Timothy 4:13. They think he may have been executed before going, or that the tradition grew out of Romans 15 itself.

debates.bearing: Scripture states the plan, not the outcome. The point of the passage does not depend on settling it: Paul planned his life around the unevangelised, and left the results to God.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 14 gives the first notable word, nouthetein, 'instruct', a verb of warning and counsel, which in the New Testament usually means setting a person's mind straight by speaking to him as a friend, as in Colossians 3:16. Paul's compliment is that the Romans are capable of doing for one another what he is about to do. Then in verse 15 he says he has written 'more boldly', tolmeroteron, and 'on some points', which in Greek is a phrase of partial extent. He is aware that in a few places he has spoken strongly, and he apologises with grace.

In verse 16 the Gentiles become an offering 'sanctified', from the perfect passive hegiasmenos. The state of holiness is a finished condition and the Holy Spirit is the one who accomplishes it. The same family of words is used in 1 Corinthians 6:11, where Paul tells the Corinthians that they were washed, sanctified and justified. So the offering is acceptable not because the Gentiles became Jewish, nor because Paul's gospel was polished, but because God's Spirit consecrates them.

Verse 18 says the Gentiles are led 'to obedience', hypakoe, and the phrase 'obedience of faith' that began the letter, Romans 1:5, is meant. The inclusio is deliberate: the letter opened and will close, 16:26, on the obedience that comes from faith. In the same sentence 'by word and deed', logo kai ergo, shows that Paul's message was never only talk.

In verse 19 he says he has 'fully proclaimed' the gospel, using plerosai, the verb of filling. Paul is not saying that everyone in the region had been converted. He means that he has filled the region with the message, planting churches in the main centres from which it could spread. Verse 20 gives his ambition with the verb philotimoumai, which comes from the words for love and honour. It is a word for a noble ambition. Paul has made an honourable point of pride out of reaching where no one else has.

Verse 26 calls the gift a koinonia, a sharing, which is the same word used of fellowship in the gospel, Philippians 1:5. Money is described with the vocabulary of communion. In verse 27 the Gentiles 'owe' it, and the verb for ministering to them is leitourgesai, from the same root as the 'minister' of verse 16. The Gentiles' service to Jerusalem is a liturgy of its own. In verse 28 Paul speaks of 'sealing' this fruit, sphragisamenos, a word for a formal act that secures the delivery, as one would seal a package or a document.

In verse 30 Paul asks the Romans to 'join me in my struggle', sunagonisasthai, a compound of the verb that gives us 'agony'. Prayer is portrayed as wrestling shoulder to shoulder in the same contest. Verse 31 asks to be 'delivered', a verb of rescue used in the Lord's Prayer, 'deliver us from the evil one', Matthew 6:13. The request is exactly what he needs to be safe, and it is not safe for him by worldly standards: he asks to be kept from unbelievers, and that his service be accepted by believers. The phrase 'by God's will' in verse 32 is meant seriously and shapes all of the plans.

typology.type: The offering of the nations, Isaiah 66:20
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah foresees survivors sent to far nations to proclaim God's glory, and the nations' people brought to Jerusalem 'as a gift to the LORD', set beside the clean vessel in which Israelites bring offerings. Paul's description of himself as a minister presenting the Gentiles as an acceptable offering reads as a purposeful fulfilment of that picture, Romans 15:16. The escalation is that the offering is not animals or grain but redeemed people, 'sanctified by the Holy Spirit'. The correspondence is therefore close, but the priesthood has changed: all believers are a holy priesthood, 1 Peter 2:5, and Paul serves as one who prepares the offering and not as an altar functionary. The type is complete in principle and still being gathered in practice.

typology.type: The wealth of the nations flowing to Zion
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 60:5 to 6 says that the wealth of the nations will come to Zion, and caravans will bring gold and frankincense, proclaiming the praises of the LORD. Paul's collection from Gentile churches to Jerusalem has a similar shape. Money moves from the nations toward the city of the temple, and the stated motive is thanksgiving to God, 2 Corinthians 9:12. The escalation is that the gift is not tribute extracted by empire but a free expression of shared life in Christ, Romans 15:27. The type falls short because Jerusalem is not the final destination. The true meeting place of the nations is the city that comes down from heaven, Revelation 21:24 to 26.

The temple was built on a foundation, and Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a precious cornerstone laid in Zion. Paul uses the image of a builder who lays a foundation where Christ has not been named, and he is careful not to build on another's work, Romans 15:20 and 1 Corinthians 3:10 and 11. The correspondence is that a community of God is built, stone by stone, on one foundation. The escalation is that the foundation is Christ Himself, and the builders are His servants, none of whom is the foundation. The type falls short because the building is made of living people, and the work is not finished until the whole structure is complete, Ephesians 2:20 to 22.

study.christ:
Christ is the grammar of this passage. The word occurs in nearly every sentence, and it is worth reading the section slowly to see how Paul deploys it.

He is the one to whom Paul belongs. 'A minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles', verse 16. The genitive is a mark of ownership. A priest in Israel served God by the appointment of the law. Paul serves by the appointment of Christ, and the gospel he serves is both 'of God' in verse 16 and 'of Christ' in verse 19. The two names stand together as in the rest of the letter.

He is the worker. Verse 18 limits Paul's speech to what Christ has done by his hands. It is a sentence of self-effacement that nonetheless claims a great deal, since it says that the risen Christ is active in the mission. 'Through me' implies that the real subject of the verb is Christ. The same thought is in Colossians 1:29, where Paul struggles with all the energy that Christ powerfully works in him. The language of 'signs and wonders' in verse 19 is credited to the Spirit, who is the Spirit of Christ, Romans 8:9.

He is the one who is not yet known. 'Where Christ was not known', verse 20. The ambition of Paul's life is to extend the name of Christ into places where it has not been spoken. The quotation from Isaiah 52:15 gives it a special weight, since Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12 is the passage about the servant who is lifted up, pierced for transgressions and bears the sin of many. Those who 'will see' and 'will understand' are those who come to grasp what the Servant has done. The gospel that Paul preaches is, in the context of Isaiah, the explanation of the Servant's work.

He is the one who gives the blessing. 'I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ', verse 29. Whatever Paul brings to Rome is not his own wisdom or his own company but a share in what Christ gives. Verse 30 appeals 'by our Lord Jesus Christ' and by the love of the Spirit, so that the entire request for prayer is grounded in His authority.

And He is the model for the gift. Paul tells the Corinthians that Christ, though rich, became poor for their sake, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and uses that to ground the same collection that Romans 15:25 to 27 describes. The Gentiles' giving to Jerusalem is a miniature of Christ's own giving. The Jewish saints had been the channel of spiritual wealth to the Gentiles, and the Gentiles return what they can. It is a picture of the body of Christ in which each part supplies the other.

The caution is that Paul himself is not Christ. The priestly language belongs to the work of making Christ known, and it does not make the apostle a mediator. The one who presents the offering to God in the end is Christ, who is the great high priest, Hebrews 4:14, and 'always lives to intercede', Hebrews 7:25.
study.god:
The first thing the passage says about God is that He gives. 'Because of the grace God has given me', verse 15. Paul does not present his mission as a career or a talent. It is a gift, and the grace that supplied the office also supplies the work. The doctrine of grace in the letter's early chapters becomes here a doctrine of vocation. God's initiative runs through the whole passage: He gives the office, the power, the sanctifying Spirit and, at the end, the journey itself, 'by God's will', verse 32.

He is also the one who receives. The offering must be 'acceptable to God', verse 16. The word turns the whole mission into worship. Paul's travels, his preaching, the churches he plants and the gift he carries are all offered to God. A reader who hears of a mission and thinks only of strategy has missed that the goal is the pleasure of God. The same thought runs through Romans 12:1, where believers are urged to offer their bodies as living sacrifices holy and pleasing to Him.

He is the Trinitarian God. The Father is the one served, the Son is the minister's Lord, and the Holy Spirit is the one who sanctifies the offering, empowers the signs and is the source of love, verses 16, 19 and 30. Paul does not list the three as a doctrine. He assumes them in the way he speaks of how mission works. The doctrine of the Trinity is practical here: it describes how a church can ask for help from every person of the Godhead in one request.

He is the God who governs plans. Paul has long wanted to come to Rome and has been 'hindered', verse 22. He does not say who hindered him, and in other places he can say that Satan did, 1 Thessalonians 2:18. Here he simply shapes his plan under the will of God, 15:32, and asks for prayer. A man with a clear ambition holds it loosely before God. That is not weakness but a form of trust that understands who is in charge of the schedule. In fact, the way things turned out, in chains and by ship, was nothing like his plan, Acts 27 and 28, and the gospel advanced all the same.

He is the God who is moved by prayer. Paul begs the Romans to struggle with him in prayer. The request is not a formality. God has linked His work in Paul to the intercession of people he has never met. The mystery of divine sovereignty and human prayer stands behind many New Testament requests, and Paul's practice is to hold both.

He is the God of peace, verse 33. The title is the verdict of the letter, which has dealt with enmity. It ends the section as it will end later paragraphs, in a benediction. For worship, the passage invites a congregation to see its giving, praying and sending as acts of worship offered to a God who receives and delights in them.

crossReferences.note: The LORD promises to send survivors to nations who have not heard His fame, and they bring brothers from all nations as a gift to the LORD, like an offering in a clean vessel. Paul's priestly language about the Gentile offering in verse 16 seems drawn from this passage.

Those who were not told will see, and those who have not heard will understand. Paul quotes it as the Scripture behind his ambition to preach where Christ was not named. It comes just before the Suffering Servant's song, so the unreached are those who will hear about His work.

Paul says that by God's grace he laid a foundation as an expert builder and that no one can lay any other foundation than Jesus Christ. It parallels Romans 15:20, and shows that his pioneering was a calling to lay the base and not a claim of superiority.

Paul hopes to preach the gospel in regions beyond the Corinthians without boasting in the work done in another man's territory. It is the same principle as Romans 15:20, stated as part of his reason for hoping their faith will grow.

At the Jerusalem meeting the leaders gave Paul the right hand of fellowship, and asked only that the poor be remembered. The request was one he was eager to fulfil. It shows that the collection of Romans 15:25 to 27 had been a commitment for years.

Paul tells the Corinthians how to set aside a weekly gift for the saints and says he will send their chosen delegates to take it to Jerusalem. It gives the practical arrangements of the collection that Romans 15 describes as nearly complete.

The service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but overflows in thanksgiving to God, and the saints will glorify God for the obedience of the givers. It explains why Paul regarded the collection as an act of worship and not merely of welfare.

Luke lists the travelling companions and records a plot as Paul was about to sail for Syria. It shows the delegates who went with the collection and the danger he had asked the Romans to pray about in Romans 15:31.

On arrival in Jerusalem, Paul reports what God did among the Gentiles, and the elders glorify God, adding that thousands of Jews have believed and are zealous for the law. The scene shows the tension that Paul hoped his service would be accepted within.

The letter's opening says that Paul has often planned to come to Rome and been prevented. Romans 15:22 to 24 supplies the reason and the change of plan, and it marks the two ends of the framework in which the whole doctrinal letter sits.

Believers are to offer their bodies as living sacrifices. In 15:16 the Gentiles themselves are the offering. The two verses together show that priestly language in Romans is used for the whole people of God as well as for the apostle's work.

The God of peace will be with those who put into practice what they have learned. It repeats the title of Romans 15:33 and ties peace with God to the way believers live, which is how the benediction in Romans is meant to be received.

study.oneStory:
The first mention of nations in the story is a promise: in Abraham all the families of the earth will be blessed, Genesis 12:3. For most of the Old Testament, that promise stays in the background while Israel's own story runs. The prophets then bring it forward. Isaiah sees survivors sent to peoples who have not heard of God's fame, and a procession of the nations into Zion, bringing their wealth and their praise, Isaiah 60:5 to 6 and 66:18 to 21. The end of the story is a worldwide worship, and Israel was always meant to be its channel.

Romans 15 is a field report from the moment when that vision begins to take shape. A Jewish apostle, a Pharisee by training, describes himself as a priest of the new covenant whose altar is the gospel, and whose offering is the converted nations. He has covered half the Mediterranean, from Jerusalem to the Adriatic. He now looks west to Spain, the edge of the known world. The directions are not accidental. The gospel moves out from Zion in widening circles, exactly as the prophets said it would, and the apostle sees himself as one of the 'survivors' sent to nations that have not heard.

The story's tensions are on show too. Paul's plan runs through Jerusalem, and the danger there is not abstract. The collection he carries is meant to heal a rift between Gentile and Jewish believers. The long conflict between the two peoples, with its roots in Babel's scattering, Genesis 11, and its long history of walls, is being addressed by a gift passing from one group to another. Reconciliation in Christ takes the form of ordinary acts: a sum of money, a ship, a prayer for safe arrival.

The ending of the story is a nation-filled city. In Revelation 21:24 to 26 the kings of the earth bring their glory into the New Jerusalem, and the gates are never shut. Paul's labour is a small part of that gathering. The offering of Gentiles that he presents is a first instalment of the harvest that will fill the city. Each church he planted, each gift sent and each prayer offered belongs to the movement that ends there, and the God of peace who sent him is the God who will finish it.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe his ministry in verse 16?

options.text: A priestly service of the gospel, presenting the Gentiles as an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Spirit.
options.note: Paul frames evangelism in temple terms, with the converted as the offering.

options.text: A purely administrative task of organizing churches.
options.note: Paul did plant and order churches, but he casts his ministry in priestly terms, presenting the Gentiles as an offering to God.

options.text: A philosophical mission to debate the wise.
options.note: His calling is priestly gospel service, not primarily philosophical debate.

options.text: A commission to offer atoning sacrifices for sin.
options.note: The offering is the redeemed nations, not a repeated sacrifice for sin.

quiz.q: What was Paul's ambition regarding where he preached?

options.text: To preach where Christ was not known, so as not to build on another's foundation.
options.note: Paul aspired to pioneer among the unreached, fulfilling Isaiah 52:15.

options.text: To minister only in well-established churches.
options.note: His ambition was the opposite, to reach places that had never heard.

options.text: To avoid all travel and settle in one city.
options.note: Paul planned extensive travel toward Spain and beyond.

options.text: To confine his work to Jewish synagogues alone.
options.note: Paul did go to the Jew first, but his ambition was frontier ground where Christ had not yet been named, among the Gentiles.

quiz.q: What was Paul planning to do before visiting Rome and Spain?

options.text: Deliver the collection from the Gentile churches to the poor saints in Jerusalem.
options.note: Paul was on his way to serve the Jerusalem believers with the relief gift.

options.text: Return to his hometown to rest.
options.note: He was heading to Jerusalem with the collection, not home to rest.

options.text: Plant a church in Illyricum first.
options.note: Paul had already preached as far as Illyricum, but his immediate plan was to carry the collection to Jerusalem before Rome and Spain.

options.text: Attend a council of the apostles.
options.note: His stated purpose was to bring the collection to the poor saints.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say the Gentiles owe material help to the Jerusalem believers?

options.text: Because having shared in their spiritual blessings, they are obligated to minister with material blessings.
options.note: Spiritual debt to Israel calls for material generosity in return.

options.text: Because Jerusalem demanded a tax from them.
options.note: It was a willing contribution, not a demanded tax.

options.text: Only because Paul personally pressured them.
options.note: The churches gave gladly and freely; the true ground Paul names is that sharing in Jewish spiritual blessings creates a joyful obligation to give materially.

options.text: Because the law of Moses required it of Gentiles.
options.note: The ground is shared spiritual blessing, not a legal requirement.

quiz.q: What did Paul ask the Roman church to pray for?

options.text: That he be delivered in Judea and that his service in Jerusalem be acceptable, so he could come to them with joy.
options.note: Paul asks them to strive with him in prayer for deliverance and a fruitful visit.

options.text: That he would gain fame throughout the empire.
options.note: He asks for deliverance and acceptable service, not personal fame.

options.text: That he would be spared all further travel.
options.note: Paul did seek deliverance in Judea, but not for the sake of ease; he longed to travel on to Rome with joy.

options.text: That the collection would make him wealthy.
options.note: The collection was for the poor saints; his prayer was for deliverance and fruitful service.

questions: Paul saw preaching the gospel as priestly service, presenting people to God as an offering. How would seeing evangelism as an act of worship reshape the way you share Christ with others?
Paul refused to speak of anything except what Christ accomplished through him. How can you keep Christ, rather than yourself, at the center of the good you do?
Paul burned to reach those who had never heard of Christ. What place do the unreached have in your prayers, giving, and imagination?
The Gentile churches gave materially to believers they had never met, out of shared spiritual blessing. Who has blessed you spiritually, and how might you respond with generosity across differences?
Paul urged the church to strive together with him in prayer for his dangerous journey. Whose gospel labors is God calling you to support in earnest, wrestling prayer this week?

translationNotes.note: Minister renders leitourgos and priestly service renders a verb for sacred, priestly work; the offering is the converted Gentiles, presented to God and sanctified by the Spirit, not a repeated atoning sacrifice.
The quotation is from Isaiah 52:15, following the Greek Old Testament, and grounds Paul's ambition to preach where Christ has not yet been named so that those who never heard may understand.
The fullness of the blessing of Christ; some later manuscripts add of the gospel, but the sense is the same, that Paul expects to come bearing Christ's rich blessing to the Roman church.
